MadeForSpace.title: Built for one room.
MadeForSpace.description: Your room fixes the dimensions. Your slab fixes the character. Neither one gets picked out of a catalogue.

items.title: You choose the actual slab
items.description: Once your deposit clears we go looking for three to five boards that suit your measurements. Each is photographed dry, then wetted so the grain reads the way it finally will. You choose from those. Nothing meets a saw before you do.
items.imageAlt: Raw walnut slabs racked in the Marrakech workshop, photographed before any cutting so the client can choose the board

items.title: Built to your dimensions
items.description: Describe the room to us, not the table. We will tell you what genuinely fits, what turns cramped the moment chairs are pulled out, and what is never getting through your doorway.
items.imageAlt: Close detail of a table edge showing the transition between timber and poured resin at full thickness

items.title: Finished by hand
items.description: Machines get the top flat. Hands take it the rest of the way. Wood and resin abrade at different rates, so the seam between them is judged with fingertips rather than eyes.
items.imageAlt: Artisan hand-sanding the wood and resin interface to an even finish at the bench

Testimonials.title: What our clients say.
Testimonials.subtitle: Every table is made for one room and one client. What they say about it belongs with the piece.
Testimonials.body: Every Benzart Resin table is made to order, one at a time, and we are still collecting written accounts from the people living with them. We would rather leave this space empty than fill it with words we wrote ourselves.
Testimonials.secondary: Until then, the work puts it more precisely than a pull-quote could. Every piece in the collection is documented with the slab it came from, the resin poured into it, and the decisions that shaped it.

atlas-walnut-river.name: The Atlas Walnut River
atlas-walnut-river.story: Sourced from the foothills of the Atlas Mountains, this slab of Moroccan walnut carries dense, unpredictable grain. The river is poured in layers of deep emerald epoxy to build genuine depth rather than flat colour, then finished with a hard-wax oil that can be spot-repaired years from now.
atlas-walnut-river.imageAlt: Rectangular Moroccan Atlas walnut dining table with a deep emerald green epoxy resin river running its full length

obsidian-grain.name: Obsidian Grain
obsidian-grain.story: The Japanese Shou Sugi Ban charring technique meets a modern deep pour. The ash is charred, brushed, and sealed, and its blackened grain sits against a light-absorbing obsidian channel. The contrast is textural rather than chromatic — both surfaces are black, and only one reflects.
obsidian-grain.imageAlt: Rectangular charred ash Shou Sugi Ban dining table with an opaque black epoxy resin channel and visible brushed grain

golden-current.name: Golden Current
golden-current.story: Ancient olive burls suspended in swirling metallic gold resin. The natural voids in the wood dictated where the resin could go, so the composition was set by the tree rather than by us. The metallic shifts as you move around it and reads completely differently under directional light.
golden-current.imageAlt: Round organic-edge olive wood table with metallic gold epoxy resin filling the natural burl voids

OurCraft.title: Our Craft.
OurCraft.description: One workshop on Ourika Road outside Marrakech, building a single table at a time for one specific room and one client.
OurCraft.philosophyHeading: We work between traditional joinery and material science.
OurCraft.philosophyBody1: Wood carries something no machine can fake: the record of one growing season, compressed into grain. Resin carries what wood cannot — depth you can look into, and a finish that can be renewed instead of replaced.
OurCraft.philosophyBody2: A table is the conversation between those two materials. Our job is making sure it is a conversation worth having.
OurCraft.studioBody1: Everything happens in one workshop in Marrakech. Boards are picked by hand. Every pour is mixed by weight rather than by eye, and every surface climbs through progressive grits before the hard-wax oil goes on.
OurCraft.studioBody2: We do not subcontract the joinery and we do not subcontract the finishing. If it carries our mark, it left our bench.
OurCraft.artisanAlt: Artisan selecting a walnut board in the workshop
OurCraft.workshopAlt: Resin being poured into a mould

phases.title: Consultation
phases.body: We talk through the room, the table, the materials and the budget. By the time the call ends you should know whether we are the right workshop for the piece — including if the answer is no.

phases.title: Design
phases.body: You get one measured drawing and a material board. No three-dimensional render, because the slab is the design and no render can tell you what the grain will do. You approve it before anything is cut.

phases.title: Selection
phases.body: Once your deposit clears we source three to five boards matching your dimensions and photograph each one dry, then wetted. You choose from those photographs. Nothing meets a saw until you have.
phases.alt: Client choosing a walnut board from photographs

phases.title: Production
phases.body: Eight to twelve weeks, depending on the season and how complex the pour is. Progress photographs come at three points: the pour, the flatten, and the first sanding coat.
phases.alt: Resin being poured into a mould

phases.title: Delivery
phases.body: In Marrakech we deliver and install ourselves. For everywhere else we crate the table in-house and hand it to a freight forwarder who specialises in fine art and furniture.
phases.alt: Table being installed in a client's home

processFaq.question: How long does a commission take?
processFaq.answer: Eight to twelve weeks from cleared deposit to delivery in Marrakech. Most of that window is cure time between resin layers, and rushing it traps heat in the pour. International freight adds transit on top, which we confirm when you book.

processFaq.question: Can I see the slab before it is cut?
processFaq.answer: You have to. Every candidate board is photographed dry and again wetted, which is the only honest preview of how the finished grain will read. You choose from those photographs, and nothing meets a saw until you have.

processFaq.question: What are your payment terms?
processFaq.answer: A deposit locks both the commission and the slab. The balance falls due before the table leaves the workshop. We do not finance pieces and we do not run staged payments after the deposit.

processFaq.question: My delivery date is fixed. Can you work to it?
processFaq.answer: Sometimes. Tell us the date in your first message rather than after we have quoted, and we will say plainly whether it is achievable. We would rather lose the commission than agree to a date we know we will miss.

processFaq.question: Do you ship internationally?
processFaq.answer: Regularly. The crate is built in-house from ISPM 15 compliant timber and handed to a forwarder who moves fine art and furniture rather than general cargo. Tracking and a packing report come with every shipment.

processFaq.question: What if it arrives damaged?
processFaq.answer: Every commissioned piece is insured from the moment it leaves the bench until somebody signs for it. One practical tip: photograph the crate before you open it. That single photo settles a freight claim faster than anything else.

Legal.privacyIntro: This policy explains how Benzart Resin collects, uses, and protects any information you give us when you use this website or enquire about a commission.
Legal.termsIntro: By using this website or enquiring about a commission, you agree to the following terms.

privacySections.heading: What we collect
privacySections.body: When you enquire, we collect your name, email address, phone number if you provide it, and the details of your project. We do not collect payment information through this website.

privacySections.heading: How we use it
privacySections.body: Your information is used only to respond to your enquiry and to prepare a quote. We do not share it with third parties, and we do not use it for marketing unless you explicitly agree.

privacySections.heading: How long we keep it
privacySections.body: We keep enquiry records for seven years to satisfy accounting and warranty obligations. After that, the record is deleted unless you ask us to keep it.

privacySections.heading: Your rights
privacySections.body: You can ask us to correct, update, or delete your information at any time by emailing the studio directly. We will respond within ten working days.

termsSections.heading: Commission
termsSections.body: A commission begins when we confirm a design and receive a deposit. The deposit is non-refundable once materials have been sourced or the pour has been scheduled.

termsSections.heading: Design ownership
termsSections.body: The final table design belongs to you. We retain the right to document the making — photographs, video, and written process notes — unless you ask us not to.

termsSections.heading: Delivery and risk
termsSections.body: Risk passes to you when the table is signed for at the delivery address. International deliveries require a signature from an adult present at the address.

termsSections.heading: Limitation of liability
termsSections.body: Our liability is limited to the replacement or repair of the table itself. We are not liable for consequential loss, including damage to surrounding property or loss of use.

Faq.title: FAQ.
Faq.description: Cost, wood, aftercare, and the work we turn down. The commissioning steps are answered on the enquiry page; this covers everything else. If your question is missing, ask us directly.

items.question: How much does a custom resin table cost?
items.answer: Most dining commissions land between 3,000 and 15,000 USD. The slab is the biggest single variable: one wide, long, well-figured board can account for over a third of the total on its own. Dimensions, resin volume, the base and the destination make up the rest. Every quote is fixed in writing before work starts.

items.question: Which wood should I choose?
items.answer: Walnut for dark, dramatic grain that suits a river pour. Olive for tight, swirling figure in shorter pieces, since long clear olive boards barely exist. Maple when you want the resin to be the loud element rather than the timber. If you are undecided, tell us the room and we will shortlist two or three.

items.question: How do I look after it?
items.answer: Wipe spills reasonably promptly and keep it out of permanent direct sun. The finish is a hard-wax oil, so a worn patch can be spot-repaired in place rather than requiring the whole top to be stripped. Refresh it every couple of years and it will outlast you.

items.question: Will the resin yellow or crack?
items.answer: Cheap resin yellows. We pour in thin layers with a UV-stabilised system, which is slower and the main reason lead times run to twelve weeks. Cracking comes from heat, not age: a pan straight off the hob will leave a permanent depression, because epoxy softens well below the temperature of a hot dish. Use a trivet and the surface is genuinely durable.

items.question: Can you copy a table I have seen?
items.answer: Not exactly, and we will not pretend otherwise. Boards from the same tree differ in density and figure, so the grain pattern belongs to the original piece. We can build another table in the same design language, at the same standard, and it will be recognisably a sibling rather than a duplicate.

items.question: What do you not make?
items.answer: No outdoor tables, since UV and thermal movement will eventually win. No flat-pack, no mass production, nothing held in stock. We also turn down commissions where the budget and the dimensions genuinely do not meet, rather than quietly cutting corners to reach the number.
